query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high-entropy alloys, the intermittent, serrated stress‐strain response at high temperatures arises from avalanche slip events that occur when the rate of applied strain exceeds the thermal healing rate of localized weak slip zones. In other words, when the strain rate is high relative to the weak spots’ healing kinetics, sudden coordinated slips occur, leading to the observed jerky mechanical and thermoelastic behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy specimens fabricated with a homogeneous microstructure that includes local slip‐weak zones (e.g., via standard processing routes such as cold rolling and annealing).
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of tensile strain rates and testing temperatures to modulate the balance between the applied loading rate and the thermal activation of defect healing.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests carried out in an inert environment across a temperature range (for example, from about 673 K to 1073 K) and a range of slow to moderate strain rates (including around 0.001 s⁻¹), ensuring that diffusion‐dominated softening does not yet occur.
generation.structural_mediator: The distribution and healing kinetics of microstructural weak zones (defects) that act as sites for avalanche slip events.
generation.mechanism: A competition between the applied strain rate and the temperature‐dependent healing (or reordering) of local weak zones: when the strain rate outpaces the healing kinetics, these zones slip collectively (an avalanche), producing stress drops. Conversely, if heating promotes faster healing relative to strain rate, the slip events become refined and the deformation appears smoother.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under conditions where the strain rate is high or the temperature is lower (reducing healing kinetics), stress–strain curves will show pronounced serrations (sudden stress drops). Conversely, at higher temperatures or lower strain rates that enhance defect healing, the deformation curve will be smoother with reduced serration amplitude and frequency.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with fewer principal elements, which do not exhibit the same pronounced balance between defect healing and strain rate, and hence display a more uniform deformation behavior without marked serrations.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when operating below temperatures where diffusion‐controlled softening dominates (e.g., below ~1073 K) and within a strain-rate regime where the kinetic competition between healing and applied deformation is critical.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative thresholds for the transition between serrated and smooth deformation regimes, as well as the activation energy for the healing process, remain uncertain and require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare tensile specimens of the refractory high-entropy alloy and concurrently test conventional alloys under identical conditions. Run a matrix of tensile tests by systematically varying the strain rate and temperature. Use in-situ high-resolution imaging (such as digital image correlation or electron microscopy) to monitor slip events and capture stress–strain behavior.
measurements: Detailed stress–strain curves focusing on the presence, amplitude, and frequency of serrations
Temporal and spatial mapping of localized slip events
Post-deformation microstructural analysis to assess the state of defect healing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental results show that the modification of strain rate or temperature does not systematically affect the occurrence or characteristics of serrated deformation (e.g., no significant change in serration frequency or amplitude across the tested conditions), or if conventional alloys display similar serration behavior under the same conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.

A series of new tensile deformation experiments is presented, which are performed at slow strain-rates on metals ranging from conventional alloys (i.e., with fewer than five principal elements) to high-entropy alloys (HEAs). HEAs are new alloys that contain at least five principal elements of roughly-equal proportion. They are high-performance materials with excellent properties for elevated-temperature applications, such as boilers and turbines. In a certain temperature and strain-rate regime, HEAs deform via sudden slips that are visible as stress drops or “serrations” in the stress-strain curves. These slips can make it difficult to precisely control the deformation behavior. Understanding how their sizes can be reduced could be used to smoothen the deformation properties, and, thus, make the deformation process more predictable and easier to control.

chosen.approach: Tensile deformation testing of high‐entropy alloys
